questions.question: What is React and why do developers use it?
questions.title: What Is React
questions.direct_answer: React is a library for building UIs from components — reusable functions that take props and return what to render. It uses a virtual DOM to minimize real DOM updates and a declarative model: you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React figures out the DOM changes.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    S[state changes] --> R[component re-renders]
    R --> NT[new element tree]
    NT --> D{Fiber diff}
    D -->|same type| U[update in place]
    D -->|different type| RM[tear down + rebuild]
    D -->|keyed children| K[match by key]
    U --> DOM[minimal DOM writes]
    RM --> DOM
    K --> DOM
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
The reconciliation model (the depth that separates candidates): React renders call your components to produce a tree of elements (a lightweight description, not DOM nodes). On state change, React calls the components again, produces a new tree, and diffs it against the previous one using the rules of the Fiber architecture — same-type elements are updated in place, different-type elements tear down the subtree and rebuild, keyed children are matched by key rather than position. Only the net DOM differences get applied.

The virtual DOM's honest cost-benefit (the follow-up that tests real understanding): the VDOM is not faster than hand-optimized DOM code — it's faster than naive full re-render. React trades a diff computation for the developer productivity of 'just re-render everything.' When that trade fails (very large trees, rapidly updating data), you reach for memoization (React.memo, useMemo), windowing (react-virtualized), or fine-grained reactive libraries (SolidJS, Svelte) that skip the diff entirely.

The hooks-era architecture (the modern picture): since 16.8, function components + hooks are the primary model. Class components still exist in older codebases but new code is functional. Hooks moved state and lifecycle into plain functions — components became closures over their props and state, which is why stale-closure bugs (useState reading an old capture) are the characteristic React bug of the era.
